title: Two Pointers
tagline: Shrink the search space without extra memory.
intro:
The two-pointers technique uses **two indices that move through a sequence in a coordinated way**, replacing a nested loop with a single pass. The payoff is dramatic: many problems that look O(n²) collapse to O(n) time and — crucially — O(1) extra space, because you carry no hash map.

The pattern shines when the data has structure you can exploit: a **sorted array** (move the pointer that can improve the answer), a **linked list** (fast/slow pointers to find the middle or a cycle), or a **partition** task (one pointer reads, one writes). When you see "sorted" plus "find a pair/triplet" or "in-place", two pointers should be the first idea you reach for.

This module covers the three concrete shapes — opposite ends, fast & slow, and same-direction — with the decision rule for which to use and the dual-language templates.
objectives: Recognise when sorted input or in-place constraints make two pointers beat hashing
Apply the opposite-ends template for pair/triplet-sum and palindrome problems
Use fast & slow (Floyd's) pointers for cycle detection and finding the middle
Use same-direction (read/write) pointers for in-place filtering and dedup
Extend two pointers to three-sum by fixing one element and scanning the rest
State why two pointers is O(n) time and O(1) space

signals: Input is sorted and you need a pair/triplet meeting a sum condition
Linked list: find middle, detect cycle, find cycle start → fast/slow
Check palindrome / compare from both ends
antiSignals: Unsorted input where you need exact value lookups → hash map is simpler
Window with a running aggregate over a contiguous range → sliding window
You need every pair regardless of order → it's genuinely O(n²)

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
Picture a sorted shelf of numbered books with one hand at each end. If the two books together are too heavy (their sum is too big), move the right hand inward to a lighter book; if too light, move the left hand inward. You close in from both sides and check far fewer pairs than trying every combination - and you carry nothing extra in your pockets.

Example: sorted `[1, 3, 4, 7]`, looking for a pair that sums to 8. Left = 1, right = 7, and 1 + 7 = 8 - found right away. If the target were 9, the 1 + 7 = 8 is too small, so move the left hand up to 3; 3 + 7 = 10 is too big, so move the right hand down - never re-checking pairs you've already ruled out.

sections.heading: The three shapes of two pointers
sections.body:
"Two pointers" is an umbrella over three distinct movements. Identifying which one you need is most of the battle.

| Shape | Pointer movement | Solves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Opposite ends** | `left` from start, `right` from end, move inward | sorted pair-sum, palindrome, container-with-water |
| **Fast & slow** | both from start, `fast` moves 2×, `slow` 1× | cycle detection, middle node, nth-from-end |
| **Same direction** | `read` scans, `write` lags behind | in-place dedup, move zeroes, partition |

The core advantage across all three: you replace a remembered set of candidates (a hash map) with the *structure* of the data, so extra space drops to O(1).

sections.heading: Which shape do I use? (decision flow)
sections.body:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Two-pointer problem"] --> B{"Linked list?"}
  B -- Yes --> C["Fast & slow (Floyd's)"]
  B -- No --> D{"Array sorted?"}
  D -- "Yes, need a pair/triplet sum" --> E["Opposite ends, move inward"]
  D -- "Modify array in place" --> F["Same direction: read + write"]
  D -- "No, need value lookups" --> G["Use a hash map instead"]
```

The single most useful trigger word is **"sorted"**. On a sorted array, comparing the sum at the two ends tells you *which* pointer to move, so you never waste a comparison.

sections.heading: Opposite-ends template
sections.body: On a **sorted** array, set `left = 0`, `right = n-1`. Compare the current sum to the target: if it's too small, the only way to grow it is to move `left` right (toward bigger values); if too big, move `right` left. Each step eliminates one element, so it's a single O(n) pass.

sections.heading: Fast & slow (Floyd's) pointers
sections.body:
Two pointers starting together, `fast` advancing two steps for every one of `slow`. After the loop, `slow` sits at the **middle** (fast reaches the end at twice the speed). If there is a **cycle**, fast eventually laps slow and they meet — that meeting is impossible without a loop, which is the whole proof.

To find the cycle's *start*: after they meet, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet again exactly at the cycle entrance.

codeExamples.label: Detect a cycle (Floyd's)
codeExamples.code:
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:        # lapped -> cycle
            return True
    return False

callouts.text: Fast & slow gives O(1) space cycle detection — no hash set of visited nodes needed. Interviewers specifically look for this over the hash-set approach.

sections.heading: Same-direction (read / write) template
sections.body: For in-place transformations, keep a slow **write** pointer marking the next slot to fill and a fast **read** pointer scanning every element. Copy only the elements that should be kept; `write` ends up as the new length. This is how you remove duplicates from a sorted array or move all zeroes to the end — in O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.heading: Extending to three-sum
sections.body: Three-sum is the canonical "two pointers inside a loop" problem. **Sort first.** Then fix each element `a[i]` and run an opposite-ends two-pointer scan on the remainder for the pair that sums to `-a[i]`. Skip duplicate values of both the fixed element and the moving pointers to avoid repeated triplets. Total cost: O(n) per fixed element × n elements = O(n²), which beats the O(n³) brute force.

interviewTalking: Lead with the property you're exploiting: "The array is sorted, so instead of an O(n²) nested loop or an O(n)-space hash map, I'll use two pointers from both ends. If the sum is too small I move the left pointer up; too big, I move the right pointer down. That's O(n) time and O(1) extra space." For linked-list problems, name Floyd's explicitly and explain why fast & slow must meet inside a cycle — that proof is the signal.
commonMistakes: Using opposite-ends two pointers on an UNsorted array (it requires order to know which pointer to move)
Forgetting to skip duplicates in three-sum, producing repeated triplets
Off-by-one in the loop condition (`lo < hi` vs `lo <= hi`) — pick based on whether an element can pair with itself
Advancing `fast` without null-checking `fast.next` in a linked list → NullPointerException
Reaching for two pointers when you really need value lookups (use a hash map)
complexityNotes: Opposite-ends and same-direction scans are O(n) time, O(1) space. Fast & slow cycle detection is O(n) time, O(1) space. Three-sum is O(n²) time (sort is O(n log n), the scan dominates) and O(1) extra space beyond the sort.
